samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 17, 2023, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approved the California Air Resources Board's (CARB) request for a waiver for its Ocean-Going Vessel At-Berth Regulation. The regulation is designed to reduce air pollution in communities near California's ports by requiring vessels to connect to shore-side power or use alternative CARB-approved emission control technology. This measure targets reductions in nitrogen oxides (NOx) and diesel particulate matter. Once fully implemented, CARB projects the rule will cut emissions from docked vessels by 90%, reduce cancer risk by 55% for residents near the Ports of Los Angeles, Long Beach, and Richmond, and generate approximately $2.31 billion in public health benefits between 2021 and 2032, including the prevention of 237 premature deaths. <2> On August 15, 2023, NOAA Fisheries implemented a final rule concerning the 2023 recreational fishing season for summer flounder, scup, and black sea bass in the northeastern United States. This ruling approved the use of 'conservation equivalency' for the summer flounder and black sea bass fisheries. Under this approach, which was recommended by both the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council and the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, federally permitted vessels are subject to the regulations of the state where they land their catch. This allows states or regions to establish their own minimum sizes, possession limits, and fishing seasons, provided they achieve the required level of conservation. For the recreational scup fishery, the rule established a 10-inch minimum size, a 40-fish possession limit, and an open season from May 1 to December 31 in federal waters, with states able to modify their own measures through the Commission process. The overall goal of these measures is to prevent overfishing while offering more tailored regulations for anglers. <3> As part of a multi-year restoration effort for the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, a project team undertook the first direct outplanting of deep-sea corals in the Gulf of Mexico. In May 2023, using a specially designed 'deep-sea elevator', the team placed nearly 200 fragments of three mesophotic octocoral species (Thesea nivea, Muricea pendula, and Swiftia exserta) on the seafloor at a depth of 230 feet. A subsequent monitoring mission by technical divers at the end of July 2023 confirmed an excellent outcome, with 95 percent of the transplanted corals having survived and appearing healthy. This survival rate is notable as the natural baseline survival for these species is approximately 92 percent annually. The expeditions in 2023, which ran from May through October, are part of a larger strategy to map habitats, develop coral propagation techniques, and restore deep benthic communities injured by the 2010 spill. <4> Throughout July and August 2023, ocean conservation was a prominent topic in U.S. environmental news, with significant developments concerning coral reefs, sea turtles, and ocean plastic removal. A major story was the unprecedented marine heatwave in Florida, which began in mid-July and caused the worst coral bleaching event ever recorded in the region. This was part of a larger, fourth global coral bleaching event confirmed by NOAA, driven by record-high ocean temperatures. In more positive news, Florida also experienced a record-breaking sea turtle nesting season in 2023, with state-wide counts for loggerhead and green turtle nests surpassing previous records. <5> In early July 2023, reports and forecasts highlighted an extraordinary and unprecedented marine heatwave in the North Atlantic, with sea surface temperatures reaching up to 5°C above normal, the warmest in over 170 years. Agencies like NOAA predicted a high probability—over 90%—that these heatwave conditions would persist through August and potentially the end of the year. These predictions were confirmed, as the extreme heat continued through September, part of a record-breaking summer for oceanic temperatures globally. The event was a manifestation of long-term, human-caused ocean warming, exacerbated by short-term factors. The intensity of the warming during the summer of 2023 was described as equivalent to two decades of warming for the region, contributing to heatwaves and flooding in Europe. <6> During the summer of 2023, an increase in shark sightings and non-fatal attacks was reported off the Northeast coast of the United States, particularly around Long Island, New York, and Cape Cod, Massachusetts. A series of bites occurred around the July 4th holiday off Long Island, prompting beach advisories and increased patrols. This trend is attributed to a combination of factors. Primarily, rising ocean temperatures, linked to both seasonal patterns and long-term climate change, have allowed sharks and their prey to expand their ranges northward into waters that were previously cooler. Additionally, successful conservation efforts have led to a rebound in the populations of both sharks, such as the great white, and their primary food sources, like seals and menhaden, bringing more sharks closer to shore. The south shore of Long Island has been identified as a nursery for several shark species, including great whites. Experts note that while encounters are increasing, sharks do not hunt humans, and many incidents are cases of mistaken identity in murky waters. The higher frequency of sightings is now considered a sign of a healthier, recovering marine ecosystem. <7> The Titan, a submersible operated by the American company OceanGate, imploded on June 18, 2023, during a tourist expedition to the wreck of the Titanic in the North Atlantic Ocean. [1, 13] The catastrophic event resulted in the instantaneous deaths of all five occupants: Stockton Rush, the CEO of OceanGate who was piloting the vessel; Paul-Henri Nargeolet, a French deep-sea explorer and Titanic expert; Hamish Harding, a British businessman; and Shahzada Dawood and his son Suleman, members of a prominent Pakistani-British family. [13, 7, 8] Communications with the support ship were lost one hour and forty-five minutes into the descent. [5, 7] This prompted a large-scale international search and rescue operation. On June 22, 2023, a remotely operated vehicle discovered a debris field approximately 500 meters (1,600 feet) from the bow of the Titanic, confirming the submersible had suffered a catastrophic implosion. [1, 10, 13] Following the incident, OceanGate suspended all exploration and commercial operations. [10] <8> After nearly two decades of negotiations, the United Nations formally adopted a new international treaty on June 19, 2023, to protect biodiversity in the high seas. [3, 6] This landmark agreement, officially titled the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), provides a unified framework for establishing marine protected areas and other area-based management tools in international waters. [3] The treaty, which opened for signatures on September 20, 2023, is a crucial step toward the global goal of protecting 30% of the ocean by 2030. [2, 4] The United States, which played a significant role in the negotiations, signed the treaty on the day it opened for signature. [1] The agreement will enter into force 120 days after 60 countries have ratified it. [3] <9> In June 2023, a significant toxic algal bloom of Pseudo-nitzschia off the coast of Southern California led to the deaths and strandings of hundreds of California sea lions and dozens of dolphins. The algae produced a neurotoxin called domoic acid, which caused neurological symptoms in the marine mammals, including seizures and death. Stranding networks, such as the Channel Islands Marine & Wildlife Institute, received over 1,000 reports of sick and dead marine mammals between June 8 and June 14 alone, primarily in the waters from Orange County to San Luis Obispo County. In response, officials and marine mammal care centers advised beachgoers to maintain a safe distance from any stranded animals, as they could pose a public health risk, and to report any sightings to rescue hotlines.

The young turtles are drawn to the jetties to feed on algae, but strong waves and coastal flooding can force them into crevices between the rocks, from which they cannot escape without help. Once trapped, the turtles are vulnerable to developing pneumonia from inhaling water and infections from shell abrasions. Mary Kay Skoruppa, the USFWS Sea Turtle Coordinator for Texas, emphasized that trapped turtles require immediate assistance from trained responders for rescue and transport to rehabilitation facilities. This is larger than the 37-year average measured size of 5,205 square miles. The dead zone is a recurring area of low oxygen that can be fatal to fish and other marine life. It is primarily caused by excess nutrient pollution, specifically nitrogen and phosphorus, from agricultural and urban runoff flowing into the Gulf from the Mississippi-Atchafalaya watershed. Trump issued a proclamation designating June 2025 as National Ocean Month. The proclamation calls upon Americans to recognize the importance of the oceans to the nation's security, economy, environment, and as a source of recreation and enjoyment. It also highlighted the administration's efforts to enhance America's maritime dominance, including actions related to offshore critical minerals, domestic seafood production, and opening the Pacific Remote Islands National Monument to commercial fishing. <2> A study released on June 3, 2025, by Dynamic Planet and National Geographic Pristine Seas, ahead of the UN Ocean Conference scheduled for June 9-13, quantifies the number of marine protected areas (MPAs) required to meet the global '30 by 30' target. [1] The report reveals a significant gap between current ocean protections and the goal of protecting 30% of the ocean by 2030. [1] To bridge this gap from the current 8% of protected ocean, the study concludes that the world must establish approximately 190,000 small MPAs in coastal areas and an additional 300 large MPAs in remote, offshore regions by the end of 2030. [1] <3> Scientists from Duke University and the University of Queensland have launched the Migratory Connectivity in the Ocean (MiCO) system, an interactive global database and map showcasing the migratory patterns of over 100 marine species. Announced on May 8, 2025, the tool synthesizes data from more than 1,300 studies to illustrate how animals like birds, mammals, turtles, and fish traverse the world's oceans, connecting almost 2,000 crucial habitats. The MiCO database is designed to bridge information gaps for policymakers and conservationists by highlighting that marine species transcend political boundaries, thus underscoring the necessity for international cooperation in conservation efforts, such as the High Seas Treaty. The project, which is a consortium of over 50 organizations, aims to provide a comprehensive, open-access baseline of marine connectivity to ensure conservation strategies are based on robust data. <4> The California Fish and Game Commission is considering several regulatory changes for ocean fishing in 2025. During its April 16-17, 2025 meeting, the Commission adopted amendments to commercial sea urchin regulations and reduced the recreational barred sand bass bag limit from five fish to four. The proposals also included considerations for the commercial take of sea cucumber and an emergency regulation for the commercial coonstripe shrimp fishery. These considerations were on the agenda for a meeting held on May 16, as federal regulations for ocean salmon fisheries also took effect on this date. <5> A March 2025 global climate news digest, primarily referencing reports from authorities like the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), detailed significant environmental changes and technological progress. The NOAA report identified March 2025 as the third-warmest March in its 176-year record, with the global surface temperature 1.31°C (2.36°F) above the 20th-century average. Ocean-only temperatures were the second warmest on record for the month. These reports highlighted the ongoing impacts of climate change on oceans, such as rising sea levels and heat content, which have been on a record-setting trend. Concurrently, the digest noted breakthroughs in aquatic research, including the use of advanced genomic techniques like eDNA to monitor species and the evolution of animal tracking technology, which now allows for more detailed monitoring of marine life and their environments. <6> A new publication titled "Marine Mammal Stranding Networks in the 21st Century: Whence and Whither?" examines the history of marine mammal stranding networks and considers their future. The paper is co-authored by Dr. Frances M. D. Gulland, Chair of the Marine Mammal Commission, along with Regina Asmutis-Silvia, Jeff Boehm, Robert A. DiGiovanni Jr., Caroline E. C. Goertz, Jessica L. Huggins, Gretchen N. Lovewell, Kathleen M. Moore, and Kristi West. The publication details significant events in the development of these networks and suggests that continued investment could improve animal welfare, advance scientific understanding, and better inform conservation and public health actions. The paper was first published online on April 12, 2025. The Marine Mammal Commission highlighted the new publication on its website on April 14, 2025. <7> The Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2025 was introduced in both the House (H.R.2860) and Senate (S.1433) on April 10, 2025. [1, 3, 4, 5] The legislation was introduced by Senators Patty Murray and Maria Cantwell, along with Representatives Rick Larsen and Emily Randall. [4] It aims to permanently reauthorize the Northwest Straits Commission and fund it with $10 million annually for six years to support the protection and restoration of marine resources in Puget Sound, Washington. [2, 4] The initiative is a community-led effort that works with local and tribal governments on projects like restoring shellfish populations and protecting marine habitats, which are considered vital for local communities, Tribes, and the state's economy. [2, 4] <8> On April 3, 2025, the 'Save Our Seas (S.O.S.) 2.0 Amendments Act of 2025' (H.R. 2620) was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives by Reps. Suzanne Bonamici, Uifa'atali Amata Coleman Radewagen, and James Moylan. The bipartisan bill aims to amend the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act to improve the administration of the Marine Debris Foundation and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Marine Debris Program. Key provisions of the legislation include authorizing the Marine Debris Foundation to establish its main office in the Washington, D.C. area or a coastal community, enhancing outreach efforts, and reauthorizing NOAA's Marine Debris Program through 2029. The amendments would also permit NOAA to use non-traditional agreements and in-kind contributions to support marine debris cleanup initiatives. A version of the bill has also been introduced in the U.S. Senate. <9> In early 2025, research highlighted the significant and accelerating impact of climate change on marine ecosystems, leading to unprecedented migration patterns and shifts in biodiversity. [1, 7] A study published on March 18, 2025, detailed how rising sea temperatures, ocean acidification, and changing currents are disrupting the historically stable migration routes of species from plankton to leatherback sea turtles. [1] This forces species to move towards cooler, deeper, or polar regions to survive. [1] These shifts create a domino effect, destabilizing food webs and impacting human communities reliant on fisheries. [1, 11] Concurrently, other research published in 2025 has focused on coral resilience. While some studies warned of catastrophic bleaching and mortality on the Great Barrier Reef due to heat stress [8], other findings offered a measure of hope. Research on rice coral, for instance, showed that it can pass heat-resisting abilities to its offspring, a key insight for breeding more thermally resistant corals for reef restoration. [2] Similarly, long-term studies in New Caledonia are working to identify specific coral species that are more resistant to thermal stress, which could help in developing targeted conservation measures. [9] <10> In a letter dated March 3, 2025, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis officially vetoed a management plan for the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary. [9] The plan, which had been finalized by the Biden administration and published in the Federal Register on January 17, 2025, was developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). [9] Its objective was to expand the existing 3,800-square-mile sanctuary and introduce new regulations aimed at protecting the area's critically threatened coral reef ecosystem. [9] The governor's veto places the future of the marine protected area in an uncertain state. [9]
